strengths: Novel module-switching mechanism with clear intuition: backdoors are localized in different modules across models, enabling effective disruption through strategic recombination
Solid theoretical foundation for two-layer networks with rigorous analysis (Theorem 1, Proposition 1) and multi-activation empirical validation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 5 datasets, 11+ attacks, 7 baselines, extensive ablations covering heuristic rules, architectures, poisoning rates, and clean data requirements

Significant practical advantages over existing defenses: works with 2 models (vs. 3-6 for WAG), requires no training data, and generalizes across Transformer/ViT/CNN architectures with single strategy
Addresses underexplored collusive attack scenario where models share backdoors, demonstrating robustness in realistic settings
Strong reproducibility: detailed setup, extensive appendix with searched strategies, promised code release, and systematic hyperparameter documentation
Consistent empirical improvements: e.g., 22.0% ASR vs. 31.9% for WAG on BadNet+InsertSent (SST-2), with especially strong results on stealthier attacks
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes two-layer networks with identity activation, while experiments use deep Transformers with ReLU/GELU. No formal justification for why module disruption in shallow linear networks should transfer to deep nonlinear models with skip connections

Heuristic design choices lack principled justification: five rules (Section 4.2) are intuitive but unmotivated; uniform λ weights (all 1.0) lack sensitivity analysis; module definitions (Q,K,V,O,I,P for Transformers) appear arbitrary; why cosine distance to WAG features optimally identifies backdoors is unproven

Limited theoretical scope: shortcut localization assumption validated only empirically, no formal robustness guarantees against adaptive attacks, gap between identity activation and complex activations used in practice

Scope limitations: explicitly restricted to classification tasks (acknowledged in Appendix A), cannot handle generative models, all tested architectures remain standard (no evaluation on SSMs, diffusion models, or emerging architectures)

Experimental concerns: improvements sometimes marginal (e.g., LWS+Hidden 40.4% vs 61.4% on SST-2), Algorithm 2's trigger invertibility assumption untested, model selection criterion lacks optimality justification, collusive attack scenario is somewhat artificial

Adaptive attack defense relies on strategy diversity as workaround (Section 5.3, Table 20) rather than fundamental robustness. Only 6.94% module overlap across strategies (Section J.5) raises questions about whether defense exploits true backdoor properties or random variation
Substantial computational cost: 2.6-4.3 hours for evolutionary search claimed as 'one-time' but represents significant overhead; inference costs not discussed

Missing analyses: no failure case exploration, sensitivity to module granularity unexplored, scalability to billion-parameter models unclear, how backdoor localization varies across model types/sizes not analyzed

strengths: Novel module-switching approach that is well-motivated by the insight that backdoors are localized shortcuts differing across models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (text and vision), architectures (RoBERTa, BERT, ViT, ResNet), and attack types (BadNet, LWS, WaNet, BATT, etc.)
Consistent empirical improvements over strong baselines (WAG, TIES, DARE) with practical advantages: works with fewer models (2 vs 3-6) and minimal clean data (20-50 samples)
Rigorous theoretical analysis for two-layer networks with Theorem 1 showing higher backdoor divergence than weight averaging, plus thorough empirical validation of assumptions
Addresses novel and realistic threat model of collusive attacks where multiple models share backdoors, where MSD remains robust while WAG degrades
Strong reproducibility with clear algorithms, detailed implementation, extensive ablation studies, and promised code release
Excellent ablation studies demonstrating importance of each heuristic rule and showing generalization across architectures and data regimes
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 only covers two-layer networks with linear activation, while experiments use deep Transformers; application via triangle inequality is straightforward

Five heuristic rules (Section 4.2) are intuitive but lack principled justification; no systematic exploration of alternative designs or theoretical grounding for specific choices like exponential decay
Candidate selection via dummy feature optimization (Algorithm 2) appears orthogonal to backdoor defense and lacks theoretical justification; Table 15 shows selection sometimes suboptimal
Limited scope restricted to classification tasks with same-architecture models, cannot handle generative models or heterogeneous collections, limiting practical applicability
Core assumption that backdoors localize in different modules across models not thoroughly explored; unclear behavior when backdoors are diffuse or when adversary adapts to known strategies
Computational cost of 2.6-4.3 hours for evolutionary search, though amortizable; scalability to billion-parameter models unclear
Some improvements are marginal with missing statistical significance testing (e.g., Table 2: 11.4% vs 12.2%); no confidence intervals across runs
Collusive attack evaluation limited to three four-model scenarios in Table 13; limited exploration of how performance degrades with more models or diverse backdoors
